newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda genocide trials to move to capital.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda genocide trials to move to capital.

text.p: The first genocide trials in the Rwandan capital open on Monday and aid officials declared on Sunday an end to an operation to repatriate Rwandan refugees from Tanzania with nearly half a million back home this month.
Those convicted on charges of taking part in the 1994 slaughter of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates face the death penalty after one chance of appeal.
"Those on trial are accused of playing a very serious role in the genocide," said Deputy Justice Minister Gerard Gahima, who declined to identify who would appear in court in Kigali.

The first genocide trials in Rwanda opened on Friday in the southeastern town of Kibungo, where Deo Bizimana, a former medical assistant, and Egide Gatanazi, a former local administrator, both pleaded not guilty to organising massacres.
Aid workers said nearly half a million Rwandan Hutus who fled to Tanzania after the genocide had returned home.
"The operation is winding down, overall it is finished," said Justin Cockerell, a delegate of the International Committee of the Red Cross in the northwestern Tanzanian town of Ngara.

"There no longer appear to be any large refugee groups," he told Reuters by telephone. "We see one or two sporadic family groups. We will be mopping up as clearly some people remain somewhere but it will be nothing like the same scale as before."
Ephreme Kabayija, director of Rwanda's commission for the repatriation of refugees, said all refugees who had fled to Tanzania in 1994 had returned to their homeland by Saturday.
Rwandan radio quoted him as saying no refugees remained in Tanzania and none were still travelling after 480,000 returned since the start of the repatriation operation on December 14.
The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said there were 540,000 Rwandan refugees in Tanzania when they were given a deadline of next Tuesday to leave by the Tanzania authorities.
Cockerell said 1,000 children found unaccompanied during the repatration were transferred to Rwanda, where aid agencies would attempt to locate their parents or relatives and reunite them.
Aid workers said some Hutu refugees were still hiding in forests in Tanzania as they refused to return home and others had been detained by troops and police while trying to escape.

More than 2,300 Hutu returnees from Tanzania this month and Zaire last month are detained on suspicion of involvement in the genocide. Some are held in protective custody to guard against mob violence.

A Hutu Rwandan refugee lobby group, the Rally for the Return of Refugees and Democracy to Rwanda, says the detained returnees are being falsely accused by people who want their property. It dismisses the trials as "a mockery of justice".
Neither defendant had defence lawyers at Friday's trial in Kibungo which lasted for only four hours. The three-judge tribunal was expected to give verdicts for both next Friday.

Foreign observers in the court said the defendants were booed and prosecutors were cheered from the crowded public benches and prosecutors passed written notes to the judges, raising doubts about the impartiality of the legal process.

Government officials say Rwanda only has small numbers of defence lawyers and most trials before the 1994 genocide went ahead without any defence representation. There are some 90,000 people crammed into jails and lock-ups accused of genocide.
Rwandans of both the Hutu majority and Tutsi minority have followed the Kibungo trial avidly over state Rwandan radio.

"These trials are an opportunity for Rwanda to look forwards instead of backwards," said Joe Felli, the Organisation of African Unity representative in Rwanda. "It means the country can be seen to be doing something about its biggest problem."
